content: Various campaigns have been implemented to highlight transformative stories of change through forums, film screenings, discussions, and awareness activities. These initiatives are often organized around village fiestas, festivals, World AIDS Day, and anti-drug events. Government-run clinics collaborating with the ROLi program provide individualized counseling and other essential services. The ROLi program has been adapted to address the needs of other vulnerable youth populations, including young women engaged in sex work and young people who inject drugs. In South Africa, the Re-Action. program, in partnership with the Department of Health, focuses on reducing new HIV infections among female sex workers and their clients in two rural districts of Mpumalanga Province. The program also aims to reduce the vulnerability of female sex workers to violence, exploitation, substance abuse, and social exclusion. This is achieved through life skills mentoring for the women, as well as community and stakeholder sensitization and outreach. A mobile clinic staffed by a nursing team provides free services, including health risk screening, counseling, HIV testing (including point-of-care CD4 testing), HIV treatment and care, and referrals to other health and social services. A 28-day calendar informs the community of emergency service availability. Nurses are trained in initiating and managing antiretroviral therapy (ART), and services, including ART and adherence support, can be provided at clients’ workplaces. Outreach workers assist clients who default on treatment by providing follow-up and support. Confidentiality is maintained by assigning outreach workers from outside the clients’ communities. Re-Action. has reached approximately 4,100 female sex workers, with a small percentage lost to follow-up due to relocation. Participants report increased knowledge of their legal rights and awareness of organizations offering support and services for sex workers. Nurses have mitigated nighttime security risks by building strong relationships with local police and brothel managers. In the USA, St. James Infirmary in San Francisco is a peer-led clinic run by and for current and former sex workers. It offers free, confidential, and non-judgmental medical and social services, including primary care, HIV and STI testing, peer counseling, hormone therapy, acupuncture, massage, support groups, needle exchange, and naloxone (Narcan) training. Supported by the Department of Public Health, private donations, and foundations, the program addresses the stigma and criminalization faced by sex workers, which often leads to inadequate or prejudiced healthcare. The clinic fosters a harm-reduction approach, creating a welcoming environment where sex workers can openly discuss their needs. Many clients are referred from other medical establishments, social service organizations, and prison programs. Outreach is conducted at strip clubs, commercial sex venues, massage parlors, and on the streets. Since 1999, over 3,500 clients have accessed care at the clinic, with an additional 30,000 contacts made through outreach and needle exchange. Many clients previously only sought emergency healthcare and now feel more comfortable accessing services tailored to their needs. The clinic also distributes resource guides on sex work, harm reduction, and transgender issues, which are used for training service providers. Annual evaluations are conducted through participant surveys and staff interviews. In Zimbabwe, the Sisters with a Voice program, run by the Centre for Sexual Health and HIV/AIDS Research (CeSHHAR), provides integrated services for sex workers across multiple sites. Collaborating with government ministries and involving sex workers in implementation, the program offers HIV testing and counseling (HTC), syndromic STI treatment, contraceptives, health education, and legal advice. Cervical screening is being introduced, with nurses trained in visual inspection and cryotherapy for pre-cancerous lesions. Peer educators conduct community mobilization sessions addressing self-worth, behavior change, contraception, HIV, cervical cancer, and advocacy. Since 2009, the program has expanded from five sites to a national network of 36 sites, serving over 14,000 women by 2013. Surveys show increased HIV testing and ART uptake among participants. In Ecuador, the Silueta X Association launched a program to promote health among young transgender individuals and prevent risks associated with non-professional feminizing hormone regimens. The project trained activists and target groups using private-sector doctors and endocrinology specialists. Peer communication and social media were key strategies for outreach. Approximately 160 young transgender individuals benefited directly. The program continues to educate on the risks of feminizing hormone regimens and incorporates this information into HIV prevention training and social events. In New York City, the Health Outreach to Teens (HOTT) program serves LGBTQ adolescents, homeless youth, and those living with HIV through an on-site medical suite and mobile unit. Services include acute and primary care, mental health services, HIV testing, case management, and health education. The program provides a trans-affirming environment, free care, and rapid appointment access. Staff are trained in transgender-competent service provision, and trans-inclusive materials are available. Weekly support groups, such as The Girls Room, engage transgender women and provide a safe space for exploration and support. A Youth Advisory Board provides feedback on services, and annual surveys evaluate the program. In India, the Pehchan program strengthens 200 community-based organizations (CBOs) to provide HIV prevention services to over 450,000 men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, and hijras. The program complements the government’s HIV prevention strategy by offering additional services that foster an enabling environment for healthy behaviors. Pehchan has developed crisis response teams to address violence and initiated a national advocacy campaign for decriminalizing homosexuality. The program’s approach has been effective in building trust and community ownership, despite societal stigma and legal challenges. These programs demonstrate the importance of tailored, community-driven approaches to address the unique needs of vulnerable populations, including sex workers, transgender individuals, and LGBTQ youth. By integrating healthcare, education, and advocacy, these initiatives improve access to services, reduce stigma, and empower communities.
